idiom_name: using guard = acquireLock(m); / await using guard = await acquire(m);
implementation_notes: TypeScript 5.2 implements explicit resource management: a using declaration calls [Symbol.dispose]() when the variable leaves scope and await using calls [Symbol.asyncDispose](), so a lock-guard object makes release structural in the same way C#'s using does, with the compiler emitting the try/finally for older targets. Pair it with an async-mutex style library (or a hand-written guard) for block-scoped critical sections, and rely on strict settings so a lazily acquired guard cannot be read before initialization. Explicit acquire/release remains for locks whose lifetime must cross function boundaries.
pitfalls: using requires an in-place initializer and a Disposable value; the syntax is downleveled, so the emit target and lib settings must be checked, and await using needs async disposal support.
Types do not change runtime semantics: on a single-threaded runtime a guard prevents interleaving, not data races - SharedArrayBuffer still needs Atomics.

Guards release in reverse order of declaration, which is convenient but hides which lock protects which invariant; two guards on one mutex deadlock, and a guard captured by a closure can outlive its scope.

variants.name: AsyncLocalStorage ambient transaction context
variants.implementation_notes: The offline-lock analogue on the Node side: AsyncLocalStorage carries the current transaction or session through every async continuation, so repositories and helpers enlist in it without being handed a transaction object - that is the 'implicit' part of Implicit Lock; run() (or the newer withScope) establishes the boundary and the framework commits or rolls back when it exits. Combine it with a transaction-aware data layer to make locking structural. Passing an explicit transaction handle stays simpler and is still idiomatic outside framework code, and work that escapes the async resource chain silently leaves the ambient context.
pitfalls: Context is lost when work escapes the async resource chain (some native add-ons, unbound event emitters, legacy callbacks): the store becomes undefined and the operation silently runs outside the transaction, i.e. unlocked.
Nested transaction() calls need an explicit join-or-independent policy, otherwise the ambient store hides the nesting and the inner boundary is a no-op.
The store is request-scoped mutable state: capturing it in timers, caches or long-lived objects leaks request state and can keep a transaction open after the response.
